introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Pure Mathematics With Statistics, Paper 3 (0770/3), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Time allowed: THREE HOURS.**

Full marks may be obtained for answers to ALL questions. Mathematical formulae and tables produced by the GCE Board are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving the answer at each stage. Electronic calculators may be used. Start each question on a fresh page.
enonce_intro_markdown: The marks obtained by candidates in a certificate examination are normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Given that 5% of the candidates scored less than 34 marks and 5% of the candidates scored more than 67 marks. Find to the nearest integer,
incertitudes: Question 6 (a) : les deux équations donnent exactement $\mu = \frac{34 + 67}{2} = 50.5$ ; « to the nearest integer » conduit à 51 (arrondi usuel de .5 vers le haut ; 50 serait défendable). Le corrigé retient 51 et $\sigma = 10$, valeurs entières demandées par le sujet.

Question 6 (c) : le sujet demande d'estimer le nombre de reçus à partir de $\mu$ et $\sigma$ « to the nearest integer ». Avec $\mu = 51$ et $\sigma = 10$ on trouve $P(X \ge 45) = 0.7257$ donc 1451 candidats ; avec les valeurs non arrondies ($\mu = 50.5$, $\sigma = 10.03$) on trouverait $0.7083$ donc environ 1417 candidats. Le corrigé donne 1451 (valeurs de (a) et (b)) et mentionne l'autre résultat ; l'écart vient de l'arrondi de 50.5.

Question 6 : la valeur critique 1.645 (table des points de pourcentage de la loi normale, $\Phi(1.645) = 0.95$) est celle des tables du GCE Board. La partie (c) n'a pas de lettre imprimée (« If 2000 candidates sat... ») ; elle est numérotée « c ». Points imprimés (7, 2, 4) : 13 au total, recopiés tels quels.

questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $X$ be the mark, $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, and $Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim N(0, 1)$.

**Lower condition.** $P(X < 34) = 0.05$, so $P\left(Z < \dfrac{34 - \mu}{\sigma}\right) = 0.05$. Since $0.05 < 0.5$ the $z$-value is negative; by symmetry the table (percentage point for a 5% tail) gives $z = -1.645$:

$$\frac{34 - \mu}{\sigma} = -1.645 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mu - 1.645\sigma = 34 \qquad (1)$$

**Upper condition.** $P(X > 67) = 0.05$, so $P\left(Z < \dfrac{67 - \mu}{\sigma}\right) = 0.95$, giving $z = +1.645$:

$$\frac{67 - \mu}{\sigma} = 1.645 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mu + 1.645\sigma = 67 \qquad (2)$$

**Solve.** Adding (1) and (2): $2\mu = 101$, so $\mu = 50.5$.

**To the nearest integer, $\mu = 51$** (exactly 50.5).

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) the standard deviation, $\sigma$, of the marks distribution.
If 2000 candidates sat for the examination and that the pass mark is 45, estimate the number of candidates who passed the examination.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use $X \sim N(51, 10^2)$ (the integer values of parts (a) and (b)). A candidate passes if $X \ge 45$:

$$P(X \ge 45) = P\left(Z \ge \frac{45 - 51}{10}\right) = P(Z \ge -0.6) = \Phi(0.6) = 0.7257$$

(table: $\Phi(0.6) = 0.7257$). Expected number of passes:

$$2000 \times 0.7257 = 1451.4$$

**About 1451 candidates passed.**

(Remark: with the unrounded values $\mu = 50.5$ and $\sigma = 10.03$, $z = -0.548$, $P = 0.7083$ and the estimate would be about 1417; the difference comes only from rounding $\mu = 50.5$ to 51.)
